strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies via roofline analysis that VLA inference is compute-bound and that the LLM backbone dominates latency, providing a solid empirical basis for targeting token pruning.

The core insight—that global attention information from previous action-generation steps can complement local per-step attention for more reliable token selection—is intuitive, supported by an illustrative hit-rate study (Figure 5) and qualitative visualizations (Figure 4, Figure 10, Figure 11).

The proposed two-level (action-level static + layer-level dynamic) pruning combined with an action-granularity-aware controller is a reasonably novel combination which directly ties pruning aggressiveness to task-relevant motion phases (coarse vs. fine-grained), an interesting VLA-specific design choice not present in prior generic VLM pruning work.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: four LIBERO task suites, comparison against three competitive recent baselines (SparseVLM, VLA-Cache, EfficientVLA), ablations isolating each of the three techniques, a design-space exploration over pruning ratio, and cross-hardware validation (A800 and RTX 3090) showing consistent speedups.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (simulation-only evaluation) and provides implementation/reproducibility details (thresholds, α values, re-implementation notes for baselines) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method involves numerous heuristically chosen hyperparameters (τ, v_th_t, v_th_r, k in rank-weighting, β=0.2 for EMA, K_G, K_D, K_base for coarse/fine modes, layer sets L_update/L_prune, pruning ratio α) that are manually tuned per LIBERO suite (e.g., α = 1.0/0.8/0.6 for different datasets). This undermines the "training-free" and general-purpose framing and raises concerns about how much re-tuning would be needed for new tasks or real robots, which is not discussed.

Evaluation is restricted entirely to the LIBERO simulation benchmark; no real-robot experiments are provided, so claims about practical deployment speedup/accuracy trade-offs remain unvalidated in more realistic, noisy settings (acknowledged only briefly as a limitation).

There are internal inconsistencies between the main text and Algorithm 1 (e.g., the frame-selection interval formula T differs in form between Section 4.2 and Algorithm 1 line 10), and some redundant/duplicated text (e.g., the "Experiment Visualization" paragraph appears twice, near-identically, once in Section 7.6 and once in the Appendix). These reduce confidence in the manuscript's polish and reproducibility of exact formulas.

EfficientVLA, one of the main baselines, is not open-sourced and was reimplemented by the authors themselves, which could introduce implementation bias favoring the proposed method; no independent verification or sensitivity check is offered.

No variance/error bars or statistical significance testing are reported despite averaging over 40–50 repeated trials, making it hard to assess whether the small SR differences (e.g., 98.2% vs. 97.6%) are meaningful versus noise.

The reported FLOPs reduction (43%) versus the achieved speedup (1.46×) suggests a fairly modest translation of theoretical compute savings into wall-clock speedup, and the paper does not analyze why the gap exists (e.g., overhead of the controller, attention-score computation, or memory movement), limiting insight into practical scalability.

The individual techniques (attention-based token pruning, temporal/global information reuse, layer-wise dynamic re-scoring) are each conceptually incremental extensions of existing ideas in VLM/VLA pruning literature (SparseVLM, EfficientVLA, VLA-Cache), so the core originality lies mainly in combining them plus the action-granularity controller, which is a reasonable but modest degree of novelty.

strengths: Strong motivation grounded in a roofline-model analysis (Fig. 1) showing that VLA inference with single-step action-chunk architectures (OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT) is compute-bound, justifying a pruning-based acceleration approach rather than memory-bandwidth optimizations.

The two key insights (hierarchical attention across layers, and spatial-temporal consistency of globally important tokens across consecutive action steps) are supported by dedicated empirical studies (Fig. 3) rather than asserted without evidence, and directly motivate the two-level pruning design.

Comprehensive experimental validation: four LIBERO task suites, two different VLA backbones (OpenVLA-OFT and π0, differing in action decoding paradigm), two GPU platforms (A800, RTX 3090), a LIBERO-plus robustness/generalization study with camera/light/background/noise perturbations, and real-world robot deployment on a 7-DoF arm across four manipulation tasks.

Extensive ablations isolating the contribution of each component (static pruning, dynamic layer pruning, action-aware controller), plus targeted studies on global attention reuse and entropy-based layer weighting that show consistent, interpretable improvements in token recall and success rate.
Detailed complexity/FLOPs analysis and overhead breakdown (Appendix A.3) showing the auxiliary computations (patch similarity, entropy) are cheap, supporting practical deployability.
Comparisons against a reasonably broad and recent set of baselines (SparseVLM, DivPrune, FastV, EfficientVLA, VLA-Cache), with method-level analysis of why each underperforms.
weaknesses: The method introduces a large number of hand-tuned hyperparameters (Kglobal, Klocal, Kdynamic, prune ratio α, similarity threshold τ, EMA rate β, velocity thresholds v_t^th/v_r^th, specific guiding layers 15 and 32, pruning layer schedule with interval T=5), many chosen empirically on LIBERO; while some sensitivity analysis is given, the overall system complexity raises concerns about how much re-tuning is needed for new robots/tasks/backbones, which somewhat undercuts the 'training-free' simplicity claim.

The absolute speedup gains are fairly modest and not clearly superior to the closest competitor: EfficientVLA achieves comparable or higher raw speedup (1.52x vs authors' 1.46x on A800) at lower FLOPs (35% vs 43%), and the paper's advantage is primarily in success-rate retention rather than acceleration itself — this should be framed more precisely rather than emphasized as a speed advantage.

Selection of the 'global' guiding layers (15th and 32nd) appears to be derived from a single illustrative task example (Fig. 3a) and then fixed as a hardcoded design choice without broader justification of why these specific depths generalize across architectures/tasks; layer indices may not transfer well to other model depths/backbones.

EfficientVLA, a key baseline, was not open-sourced and had to be reimplemented by the authors, which could bias the comparison (intentionally or not) in the proposed method's favor; no independent verification of this reimplementation's fidelity is provided.

Reported FLOPs-reduction figures show minor inconsistency between the main text (57% FLOPs, i.e., 43% retained per Table 1) and the appendix complexity analysis (63% reduction, i.e., 37% retained), which is a small but avoidable discrepancy affecting reproducibility clarity.

The real-world evaluation, while a valuable addition, is based on a small number of trials per task (task success rates reported without confidence intervals) and only four tasks with a single robot platform, limiting statistical confidence in the 1.70x real-world speedup and success-rate parity claims.

The paper is dense with many closely related formulas, ablations, and hyperparameter tables spread across a long appendix; the core contribution could be presented more concisely, and some claims (e.g., 'negligible success rate degradation') are asserted based on small differences within typical LIBERO run-to-run variance, which is only partially quantified in Table 12.

strengths: The paper is grounded in clear, well-validated empirical observations (hierarchical attention across layers, spatial-temporal consistency of important tokens across consecutive action steps) that directly motivate the design choices, rather than being purely heuristic.

Extensive experimental validation: multiple LIBERO task suites, two structurally different VLA backbones (OpenVLA-OFT and π0), five competitive baselines, cross-hardware evaluation (A800 and RTX 3090), a robustness study on LIBERO-plus with perturbations, and—notably—real-world robot deployment on a 7-DoF arm with three camera views across four manipulation tasks, which is uncommon and valuable evidence of practical applicability.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (static global pruning, dynamic layer pruning, action-aware controller, entropy-based layer weighting) with both recall-rate and success-rate metrics, helping substantiate the causal story behind the method's effectiveness.

Training-free design with detailed complexity/FLOPs analysis and overhead breakdown (e.g., patch similarity and entropy computation costs), supporting reproducibility and practical deployment considerations.

Additional generalization check of the action-mode (coarse/fine-grained) recognition mechanism on a different model (UniVLA) and simulator (SimplerEnv) with a different robot arm, strengthening the claim that the core insight is not overfit to one platform.
weaknesses: The method combines many hand-tuned hyperparameters (Kglobal, Klocal, Kdynamic, τ, β, velocity thresholds v_th_t, v_th_r, frame-selection constants k and b) that are calibrated on LIBERO/OpenVLA-OFT; although some robustness ranges are reported, the overall sensitivity of end-to-end performance to joint mis-calibration across a new robot/task is not fully explored.

The real-world evaluation, while a strong positive, is limited to four tasks with a small number of demonstrations/trials, so the statistical reliability of the reported success rates and speedup is hard to assess (no variance reported for real-world runs, unlike the simulation experiments).

EfficientVLA, one of the strongest speed baselines, is not open-sourced and had to be reimplemented by the authors based on paper details, which raises some concern about the fairness/accuracy of this comparison.
SP-VLA is discussed as closely related work but is not included as an empirical baseline, leaving a gap relative to a directly comparable contemporary method.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines known ideas (temporal/token caching, attention-based importance scoring, layer-wise dynamic pruning, early-layer speculative attention) into a well-engineered pipeline rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the main new element is the action-aware velocity-based controller.
The manuscript is notation- and figure-heavy with substantial content deferred to a long appendix, which somewhat hurts the self-containedness and readability of the main text.
